summary: Proposes an extension to HTML so that information providers can ask users to upload files in forms, plus a MIME-compatible way to carry the upload. It is experimental, now historic, and was replaced by RFC 2854.

eli5.summary: A way for a web page to include a button that lets you pick a file from your computer and send it.

questions: how does html file upload work
how do web forms send files
subtitle: The mechanism for web forms to accept files from users and a MIME encoding for sending them back to servers.

tldr.problem: HTML forms let users fill in text fields but provide no way to ask users to submit files. Web services needing files from users had to build custom applications.
tldr.mechanism: Add a FILE input type to HTML forms and define multipart/form-data, a MIME encoding that lets browsers send form fields and file contents together in a single request body.
tldr.outcome: File upload became a standard web capability. This RFC is historic and was replaced by RFC 2854.

today: RFC 2854 obsoletes this RFC. File upload is now a standard web capability, widely supported and used for document submission, image uploads, and data import across the web.

sections.title: Adding File Upload to HTML Forms
sections.content:
HTML forms could ask users for text input (names, passwords, search terms) but not for files. A form designer who wanted to collect user files had to direct users to custom applications, losing the simplicity of browser-based forms.

This RFC proposes two changes to HTML: add a FILE option for the TYPE attribute of <INPUT> elements, and define a new MIME type, multipart/form-data, to let browsers send form data and files efficiently. A form author simply writes <INPUT TYPE="file" NAME="document"> and the browser handles file selection and transmission.
sections.eli5: HTML forms used to let you type things but not pick files. Now they do.

sections.title: The FILE Input Type and multipart/form-data
sections.content:
When a browser encounters <INPUT TYPE="file">, it displays a button (often labeled "Browse") that opens a file picker. The user selects one or more files. When the form is submitted, the browser reads the files and sends them together with other form fields as a single HTTP POST request.

The encoding type application/x-www-form-urlencoded (used for regular text forms) is inefficient for binary or large data. Instead, multipart/form-data sends the request as separate sections ("parts"), each with a boundary marker to separate them. Each part includes a Content-Type header describing its content (text/plain, image/gif, etc.) and the actual data. This is similar to how email attachments work.
sections.eli5: The browser shows a 'Browse' button. You pick a file, the browser packages it up with the other form fields, and sends everything as a multi-part mail message.

sections.title: Multipart Form Encoding
sections.content:
A multipart/form-data request begins with a boundary—a unique string that does not appear in the data. Each form field is sent as a separate part with a Content-Disposition: form-data header specifying the field name. Text fields and file fields are treated uniformly. File parts include a filename parameter preserving the original file name, and a Content-Type header (e.g., text/plain or image/jpeg) if known.

If a user selects multiple files for a single field, they are sent as multipart/mixed, which is a multipart section within the form-data. Servers parse the boundary, extract each part, validate it, and write files to storage for processing. This structure handles text, binary, and mixed data uniformly.
sections.eli5: The data is divided by a marker, like pages in a letter. Each part says 'this is field X' or 'this is the file named Y.' The server reads it back out and saves the files.

sections.title: Browser and Server Guidance
sections.content:
Browsers should let users select one or more files, optionally constrain file selection by media type using the ACCEPT attribute, and handle files larger than might fit in memory by streaming them. Older browsers that do not support file input will treat <INPUT TYPE="file"> as a text field, letting users type a path.

Servers should check the Content-Type header and be prepared for the request to arrive as either multipart/form-data (new browsers) or application/x-www-form-urlencoded (old browsers). For backward compatibility, a server can respond to the old encoding by sending a helper application type that client-side code can use to retry with the correct encoding. The RFC includes examples of both single and multiple file submissions.
sections.eli5: Browsers need to let users pick files and send them properly. Old browsers will need help. Servers should accept both old and new ways.

sections.title: Trust and User Control
sections.content:
A user agent must never send a file the user did not explicitly select. In particular, a form must not use hidden fields to specify file names or paths; only visible file input fields may be used. Browsers should confirm any default file names suggested with the VALUE attribute before uploading.

Once uploaded, the server is responsible for handling the file securely. The RFC does not address encryption of the upload itself; that should be handled by secure HTTP (HTTPS) or other transport-level security. Servers should also validate file size, type, and content before storing.
sections.eli5: Never sneak a file upload without asking the user. Once the server gets the file, it has to be careful with it.
